claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential combined with two-phase coexistence molecular dynamics can accurately predict melting properties of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The predicted properties include melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The combined approach is suitable for high-throughput calculations.
The initial material is a representative refractory high-entropy alloy with a stable solid-phase microstructure, uniform elemental distribution, and minimal impurities.
The interatomic potential should be trained on DFT data covering the relevant high-temperature range.
A two-phase molecular-dynamics protocol can model solid-liquid coexistence and extract melting properties.
Simulations may need to extend to approximately 3000 K or above to cover the expected melting range.
Simulation cells must be large enough to stabilize concurrent solid and liquid phases.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit chemical short-range ordering.
A machine-learning interatomic potential can represent effects associated with short-range order in an RHEA.
The learned potential captures local atomic-environment variations relevant to melting.
A highly accurate machine-learning interatomic potential can support molecular-dynamics simulations of an RHEA over a wide temperature range.
The machine-learning potential closely approximates the ab initio energy surface with sufficient fidelity to track melting transitions.
The two-phase method directly simulates thermodynamic equilibrium between solid and liquid and thereby determines melting properties.
The method will predict melting temperature within tens of kelvin to approximately 100 K of experiment or established ab initio benchmarks.
The method will accurately predict enthalpy and entropy of fusion and volume changes at melting.
The method costs only a fraction of full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
Accuracy depends on the coverage and quality of the DFT training database, and extrapolation beyond represented compositions or temperatures may be less reliable.
Systematic DFT errors, partial ordering, and finite simulation-cell size are sources of uncertainty.
Deviation of the predicted melting temperature by more than 100 K from experimental or ab initio reference values would falsify or require revision of the accuracy hypothesis.
